title: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
desc: Distinguishes purchasing, engagement and effective use while comparing peer support, champions, mandates and experimentation.

kps.k: The central proposition is that legal AI creates organisational value through sustained use, workflow redesign and implementation support—not software access alone.
kps.d: Harvey’s leaders describe a shift from an individual lawyer copilot toward infrastructure for firmwide and in-house deployment. Practitioner accounts locate the implementation challenge in turning useful personal experiments into repeatable team practices. Bazin at Lewis Silkin advocates shared default workflows; Torys’ announcement commits onsite legal engineers to practice-specific development. These accounts offer an operational theory of transformation, while deployment announcements establish commitments rather than achieved service improvements.

qs.q: But they’re often doing so individually — which means the next step is turning that experimentation into more structured, group-level adoption to drive scale and return.
qs.a: Harvey Power Users: The Champions Network — Alex Bazin at Lewis Silkin · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: “As we’ve scaled, really the value prop that we want to sell to law firms is we will make your business better.”  This shift means focusing on platform capabilities that improve firm profitability through better client matter management, workflow optimization, and direct collaboration between law firms and their clients on Harvey’s platform.
qs.a: Lessons from Slush 2025: How Harvey Is Scaling Domain-Specific AI for Legal and Beyond · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: Purchasing, active engagement and effective use remain distinct measures of adoption.
kps.d: A&O’s early trial reportedly involved roughly 3,500 lawyers and 40,000 queries, but those figures did not establish accuracy or productivity. In June 2026, Bazin reports monthly engagement by two-thirds of Lewis Silkin users, with about half of that group active at least weekly. Roberts and Wilkins contrast broad licensing with a highly engaged minority, citing Harvey’s 75–85% daily activity figure specifically for users adopting at least four product lines. Their assessment of uneven adoption and the customer studies’ reports of expanding use concern different populations and measures; neither establishes profession-wide penetration or a causal effect of broader product use.

qs.q: We’re told that at the end of the trial, around 3,500 of A&O’s lawyers had asked Harvey around 40,000 queries for their day-to-day client work.
qs.a: Allen & Overy breaks the internet (and new ground) with co-pilot Harvey · Market & press · 2023

qs.q: Two-thirds of our users engage with Harvey monthly, and about half of those use it at least weekly.
qs.a: Harvey Power Users: The Champions Network — Alex Bazin at Lewis Silkin · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Power-user definitions expose a disagreement about whether usage volume signals value or obscures it.
kps.d: Díez Tomillo distinguishes frequent users from those producing better outputs or discovering new applications: only six or seven of Repsol’s approximately 30 tracked power users satisfy both definitions. Whittaker at Burges Salmon prioritises workflow fit, execution and client needs, including choosing not to use AI. Salajan at Schoenherr treats sustained voluntary engagement by sceptical lawyers as an initial signal of value, alongside complex-feature use and knowledge sharing. The practical distinction is between using activity data to identify opportunities and treating prompt counts as proof of quality or outcomes.

qs.q: Out of 150 users in our legal team, we're following about 30 power users, and about six or seven satisfy both definitions.
qs.a: Harvey Power Users: 'People Call Me Harvey' — Javier Díez Tomillo at Repsol · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: But measuring [adoption](/blog/turn-ai-adoption-into-firm-wide-change) purely by prompt volume doesn’t reflect quality or outcomes.
qs.a: Harvey Power Users: The Purposeful User — Tom Whittaker at Burges Salmon · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Peer networks and specialist support offer a route from individual proficiency to collective capability, but champions need not be technical experts.
kps.d: Lewis Silkin embeds champions, often knowledge lawyers, within practice groups and uses demonstrations across seniority levels. Repsol combines a testing taskforce with informal exchanges; Schoenherr offers early access and projects in return for feedback. Bazin separates the champion’s adoption-support role from advanced use, while Whittaker recommends accessible team-level experts rather than expecting everyone to become a specialist. Axiom’s Saretto adds an ALSP perspective: lawyers can coach in-house colleagues through live work. These are reported practices and proposed mechanisms, not comparative tests of training effectiveness.

qs.q: Champions don’t need to be the most advanced users themselves.
qs.a: Harvey Power Users: The Champions Network — Alex Bazin at Lewis Silkin · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: Ideally, you’d have one power user per team so that when people are listening to what that sector or those clients need, they can identify where the technology could help.
qs.a: Harvey Power Users: The Purposeful User — Tom Whittaker at Burges Salmon · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Adoption strategies differ over mandates, experimentation and the time needed to learn.
kps.d: Harvey’s LaBarre recommends mandated use for identified tasks; Markel uses directional usage tracking, and Adecco includes volume and higher-value experimentation in KPIs. Other practitioners stress persuasion and personally experienced benefits rather than compliance. Shaver favours brief daily experimentation without prescribing every use case. Later accounts emphasise protected learning time, contrasting with A&O’s 2023 claim that brief tips sufficed for rollout. Dressler describes an initial learning and verification J-curve, whereas SenGupta reports immediate gains among study participants. These experiences do not establish a universal learning period. Nor does age settle proficiency: Díez Tomillo tentatively associates youth with adoption, while Bazin reports no generational divide and highlights senior lawyers’ agency and ability to assess outputs.

qs.q: They need to identify use cases, mandate that these tools be used, and set expectations around how and on what folks are expected to be using AI.
qs.a: How our In-House Legal Team Uses Harvey to Work Smarter · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: It follows more of a J-curve — you’re experimenting, validating outputs, and building trust.
qs.a: Harvey Power Users: The Skill You're Sharpening — Bryan Dressler at Markel · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Customer research reports substantial time savings, but definitions, selection and measurement limit broader conclusions.
kps.d: The November 2025 Harvey-commissioned RSGI study covered 29 law firms and 11 in-house teams, predominantly experienced customers. It reported monthly savings of 36.9 hours for law-firm power users versus 15.7 for standard users, and 28.3 versus 11.8 in-house. Participants defined power use themselves, and savings were mostly estimates. Later articles and interviews reuse these findings rather than provide independent replications. RSGI’s April–June 2026 research, reported by Legal IT Insider as independently conducted despite Harvey’s commissioning, covered 87 unique respondents and reported 11 weekly hours saved by law-firm power users. These findings describe participating customers, not causal effects or standardised performance across the profession.

qs.q: The final data from the report shows that law firm power users save 36.9 hours a month using Harvey and standard users save 15.7 hours.
qs.a: The Impact of Legal AI — A deeper dive into the RSGI/Harvey adoption report · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: “[The Accelerating Impact of Legal AI: Harvey as Foundational](https://www.harvey.ai/resources/reports/accelerating-impact-of-legal-ai)” draws on research conducted between April and June 2026, comprising 87 unique respondents across 60 firms and 27 in-house teams.
qs.a: RSGI's second Harvey report shows jump in adoption · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The claimed benefits extend beyond speed to analytical depth, capacity and professional development, without establishing employment effects.
kps.d: Document-heavy diligence, extraction, drafting and review supply the main practical examples. Howell at Foley & Lardner and Dressler at Markel say saved time permits deeper scrutiny rather than simply faster completion. Harvey’s mid-sized-firm accounts describe handling more matters without adding staff and involving associates earlier in strategy. SenGupta reports positive workplace-fulfilment responses from 83% of study participants, but retention and accelerated learning remain interpretations or testimonials rather than measured outcomes. The June 2026 study reports that 69% of firms do not plan to reduce graduate intake over two years; this is a staffing intention, not proof that augmentation will prevent displacement.

qs.q: We can then use that time to tighten our analysis and provide additional insights.
qs.a: Harvey Power Users: The 'Aha!' Moment — Chanley Howell and Kelly Boyd at Foley & Lardner · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: So it’s not just about efficiency, it creates the opportunity to do a deeper level of analysis.
qs.a: Harvey Power Users: The Skill You're Sharpening — Bryan Dressler at Markel · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Time savings do not automatically become financial returns or lower client bills.
kps.d: Early RSGI reporting acknowledges immature ROI frameworks. Pereyra proposes examining written-off work and specialised client workflows because a horizontal assistant’s financial contribution is difficult to isolate. The June 2026 study reports higher utilisation, revenue and profitability among firms able to track changes, without demonstrating causation. Buyer and provider accounts also diverge: 61% of firms report proactive efficiency discussions, against 4% of in-house teams reporting approaches from their firms; only one in-house team reports savings resulting from mandated outside-firm AI use. Earlier reports of reduced external spending through insourcing concern a different mechanism. Roberts and Wilkins identify hourly-billing tensions, while Law & Order: GPU recommends fixed-fee or contingency workflows where efficiency better aligns incentives.

qs.q: But…  I think a lot of it is localizing it to practice areas because I think the big challenge is when you use Harvey as a horizontal assistant, it’s hard to map this to ROI.
qs.a: The Models Are the Product: Gabe Pereyra on Building an AI Associate and Matter-Centric Workflows · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: Among firms able to track changes, 59% report increased lawyer utilisation, 44% increased revenue, and 53% increased profitability in lawyers that use Harvey.*  *• Value is now measured in better legal and commercial outcomes, a significant leap from six months ago.
qs.a: RSGI's second Harvey report shows jump in adoption · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Custom workflows, agents and shared workspaces extend the adoption thesis toward reusable expertise and new service models.
kps.d: Harvey reports more than 18,000 custom workflows following its June 2025 release and more than 25,000 custom agents by May 2026. Its agent library and builder aim to encode organisational precedents and processes; Microsoft integrations and matter workspaces aim to reduce fragmented context. Shared Spaces extends the proposition across firms, clients and internal functions. Pereyra reports firms beginning to offer implementation help to smaller in-house teams, and Roberts and Wilkins describe revenue-sharing experiments around commercialised workflows. Activity counts and product launches establish neither reliable end-to-end delivery nor realised new revenues; customer collaboration testimonials often remain exploratory.

qs.q: Since the release in June, Harvey customers have built 18,000+ custom workflows.
qs.a: Harvey's Top 5 Product Releases of 2025 · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: "Now every legal team can do the same: take what makes their practice distinctive and turn it into agents that scale."  Legal teams have created more than 25,000 custom agents on Harvey.
qs.a: Built by Lawyers, Tailored by You: Harvey Launches Purpose-Built Legal Agents Across Every Major Practice Area · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Human verification and institutional governance remain conditions of deployment, despite increasingly autonomous product language.
kps.d: Foley practitioners require thorough review before client delivery, and Harvey’s internal DORA example describes checking outputs against contract language. Platform accounts emphasise ethical walls, permissions, audit logs and data separation; these controls address confidentiality, not substantive correctness. Harvey’s May 2026 agent announcement reserves judgment for lawyers despite promising near-one-click deliverables. Its testing claims provide no scores in the supplied excerpt. Likewise, BigLaw Bench is Harvey’s own benchmark and its 2024 announcement acknowledges incomplete lawyer-task performance. Founder claims of citation reliability and attorney preference do not establish independently measured hallucination rates. The practical implication is to specify verification and access controls within each workflow rather than infer safety from adoption or branding.

qs.q: But just like any work, it needs to be thoroughly reviewed prior to having a client-ready version.
qs.a: Harvey Power Users: The 'Aha!' Moment — Chanley Howell and Kelly Boyd at Foley & Lardner · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Harvey’s platform strategy offers a proposed competitive advantage, not a settled market outcome.
kps.d: Supporters attribute differentiation to legal expertise, customer-led implementation, trusted content, governance and integration rather than model intelligence alone. Law & Order: GPU separately identifies brand-led purchasing and cautions against equating it with a product network effect. Roberts and Wilkins leave workflow portability, retention and competition from foundation-model providers unresolved; they also identify Legora’s competing enterprise strategy. Another company analysis reports Harvey abandoning its proprietary legal model after frontier models surpassed it on Harvey’s own benchmark, qualifying older custom-model defensibility claims. In-house procurement commentators add that existing enterprise AI subscriptions may reduce demand for a separate legal platform. Commercial growth therefore does not settle comparative efficacy, durable advantage or benefits to law firms themselves.

qs.q: “We think of a lot of the product as not going to be the models, it’s going to be all of the infrastructure around them,” Pereyra noted.
qs.a: Lessons from Slush 2025: How Harvey Is Scaling Domain-Specific AI for Legal and Beyond · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: The product itself may not (yet) have a network effect – one lawyer using Harvey doesn’t inherently make another lawyer more effective, the way one new user might improve a social network or a file-sharing platform.
qs.a: Law & Order: GPU · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: The supplied traditional law-firm source accepts the proposition’s core and extends it with a concrete implementation model: A&O Shearman is not presenting software access alone, but firm-specific agentic workflows built through collaboration among its lawyers, Harvey and Microsoft. Across the announcement, the shared rationale is that embedding legal expertise into repeatable workflows can simplify complex work and substantially reduce completion time. There is internal variation in emphasis: David Wakeling focuses on concrete use cases and speed; firm partners stress simpler output and better work; Harvey’s CEO adds claims about preserving accuracy and trust. Those claimed benefits are promotional participant endorsements, however, with no independent performance measurement, adoption evidence, verification methodology or demonstrated organisational and financial outcomes in the supplied excerpt. This is evidence from one curated joint announcement and should not be treated as representative of traditional law firms generally.

qs.q: In 2023, A&O Shearman became the first firm globally to build an AI app for in-house counsel by collaborating with Harvey and Microsoft to create ContractMatrix, an AI-powered contract tool.
qs.a: A&O Shearman and Harvey to Roll Out Agentic AI Agents Targeting Complex Legal Workflows · Law firms · 2025

qs.q: Together with A&O Shearman, Harvey is building agentic workflows that save tremendous amounts of time without sacrificing accuracy and trust.
qs.a: A&O Shearman and Harvey to Roll Out Agentic AI Agents Targeting Complex Legal Workflows · Law firms · 2025

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech-vendor sources collectively accept the principal proposition and materially develop it into an implementation model. They distinguish licences and activity counts from effective use, and locate organisational value in practice-specific workflow redesign, sustained experimentation, training, peer champions or legal engineers, governance, human verification, and integration with existing work systems. They further extend the proposition toward reusable agents, shared cross-organisational workspaces and implementation services that may support new service models. Material variation concerns how adoption should be driven: some advocate mandates, targets and usage tracking, while others favour voluntary experimentation, peer influence and visible benefits; some treat sustained engagement as an initial signal of value, while others warn that prompt volume can obscure quality and outcomes. Sources also vary in evidential strength. Practitioner accounts report task-level savings and deeper analysis, but much of the broader evidence consists of vendor-reported estimates, customer testimonials, deployment plans and product claims rather than independent causal evaluation. A few sources redirect attention toward model capability or benchmarking, or provide too little adoption evidence to determine a position, but they do not outweigh the professional voice’s overall implementation-centred contribution. This describes the supplied curated sources only and does not establish how prevalent these views are among legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: But measuring [adoption](/blog/turn-ai-adoption-into-firm-wide-change) purely by prompt volume doesn’t reflect quality or outcomes.
qs.a: Harvey Power Users: The Purposeful User — Tom Whittaker at Burges Salmon · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: "As more clients adopt platforms like Harvey, we are able to meet them in those same environments and work more seamlessly together, reinforcing that the value of these technologies depends on how they are integrated into workflows, governed appropriately, and applied with a clear focus on outcomes."  "Our agents aren't designed by prompt engineers.
qs.a: Built by Lawyers, Tailored by You: Harvey Launches Purpose-Built Legal Agents Across Every Major Practice Area · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an:
Taken as a curated set rather than a representative survey, these market-analyst, consultancy and press sources generally accept the proposition that purchasing Harvey or recording high activity does not by itself establish organisational value. They repeatedly distinguish enterprise rollout, seat or query counts and power-user activity from effective use, measured outcomes and financial returns. Their common explanation is that value depends on embedding AI in existing legal work, developing reusable workflows, building user fluency and providing implementation infrastructure and support. The voice materially extends the proposition by identifying additional enabling conditions: guided onboarding, embedded legal engineers, content and document-system integrations, human verification, access controls for agentic workflows, and pricing or workflow choices that align efficiency with provider economics.

Material internal variation concerns both strategy and evidence. Some sources favour daily, lightly prescribed experimentation to develop sophisticated users, while others stress top-down procurement, mandates or guided product design. Some treat power-user activity as a useful early signal; others emphasise that heavy users need not redesign workflows or become change champions. Customer studies report substantial estimated time savings and later commercial outcomes, but their commissioned, customer-only samples, self-defined power users and immature ROI methods limit causal or profession-wide conclusions. Other reporting redirects attention to firm size, existing enterprise AI subscriptions and procurement coordination, while early-stage or vendor-market commentary provides too little implementation evidence to take a clear position. There is also tension between optimistic claims that adoption can be quick and inexpensive and accounts emphasising sustained learning, specialist support and governance. Overall, the sources develop a more concrete implementation and incentive framework around the proposition without establishing that any single approach reliably produces quality, ROI or lower client costs.

qs.q: Often those conversations go something like: “So, how are the lawyers at Big Firm X actually using Harvey day-to-day?” The answer, more often than not, is: “Well, they’re not really using it much… yet.” It might sound underwhelming – by many accounts, Harvey isn’t (at this stage) deeply embedded in most lawyers’ daily workflows.
qs.a: Law & Order: GPU · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research source supports the proposition that software access and licence adoption are inadequate measures of organisational value. Roberts and Wilkins distinguish purchasing from actual use and argue that the stronger test is whether Harvey becomes integrated enough to reshape legal workflows. They also identify a highly engaged minority, suggesting that power-user behaviour may reveal more than aggregate adoption statistics. Material variation lies in the source’s caution: it treats deep engagement as a promising signal rather than proof of effective use, productivity or firmwide transformation, and leaves workflow portability, platform stickiness and broader product-market fit unresolved. Its discussion of custom workflows and governance provides strategic context, but does not establish measured organisational outcomes. Because this is one jointly authored source in a curated corpus, it should not be treated as representative of academia or research generally.

qs.q: One word of caution: adoption in terms of licenses is reportedly high, but actual use apparently remains relatively low.
qs.a: Harvey's Strategic Evolution · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Harvey hasn't yet created the kind of pull where the tool reshapes how you work rather than slotting into how you already work — the kind of pull that is an unmistakeable sign of product-market fit at the use level rather than the purchasing level.
qs.a: Harvey's Strategic Evolution · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: The supplied source supports the proposition that legal AI creates organisational value through developed capability and governed implementation rather than software access alone. Pereyra rejects the idea that AI can simply be substituted into existing work, emphasising substantial differences in user skill, and describes Harvey’s evolution from an individual productivity tool toward firm-wide deployment infrastructure addressing security, privacy, governance, ethical walls and regulatory requirements. There is a material qualification: he treats frequency of use as distinguishing successful partner adopters, whereas the cluster cautions that usage volume alone may obscure output quality and realised value. This is a tension over measurement, not a rejection of the central proposition. The evidence is also principally Pereyra’s company and product account, based on observations and stated platform objectives rather than quantified outcomes or an independent regulatory assessment; it should not be treated as representative of regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

qs.q: People sometimes talk about AI as something you “swap in,” but it’s much more like a personal computer or the internet.
qs.a: Harvey's Gabe Pereyra on the Future of Legal AI · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: A lot of the product and platform problems you need to solve are not just, “How do you build a good product for an individual lawyer?”  It’s all of the security, data, privacy, governance, ethical walls—all of the regulatory challenges—everything you need so that a large law firm can use this with confidence.
qs.a: Harvey's Gabe Pereyra on the Future of Legal AI · Regulators & courts · 2026

elens.an: The 2015–2022 source is broadly compatible with the proposition but does not directly establish or contest it. It reports that Harvey was already being used across several kinds of legal organisations and relays predictions that it could improve quality, efficiency and access. However, it explicitly characterises the product as being in its early days and provides no evidence about sustained engagement, workflow redesign, implementation support, verification practices, productivity, or organisational returns. Privacy controls and access to OpenAI and Microsoft resources address deployment readiness rather than effective use. Internal variation is therefore mainly evidential: reported early adoption and optimistic investor expectations point toward potential value, while the small team, undisclosed revenue and absence of measured outcomes leave the proposition unresolved. As this is a single curated source, it should not be treated as representative of commentary from the period.

qs.q: “We believe Harvey will have a transformative impact on our legal system, empowering lawyers to provide higher quality legal services more efficiently to more clients,” Lightcap said via email.
qs.a: Harvey, Which Uses AI to Answer Legal Questions, Lands Cash from OpenAI · Market & press · 2022

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources generally support the proposition by separating broad access and engagement from demonstrated organisational value. Reports of A&O’s firmwide rollout and high query volume establish substantial early use, but do not independently measure accuracy, productivity, client outcomes or financial returns. At the same time, accounts of firm-specific fine-tuning, workflow integration, confidentiality controls and lawyer review indicate that deployment required organisational and technical implementation beyond purchasing software. Material variation lies in emphasis and evidential strength: the A&O rollout reports most directly support the access-versus-value distinction; promotional accounts from Harvey, OpenAI and A&O predict efficiency, quality and higher-value work but provide mainly attributed testimonials or lawyer preferences; and BigLaw Bench addresses task performance and acknowledges incomplete lawyer-task completion without examining sustained adoption or realised organisational value. One limited counterpoint is A&O’s claim that users needed only brief guidance, but this does not displace the broader evidence of firm-specific implementation and unresolved verification procedures.

qs.q: By the end of the trial, some 3,500 A&O lawyers had asked Harvey around 40,000 queries for their day-to-day client work.
qs.a: As Allen & Overy Deploys GPT-based Legal App Harvey Firmwide, Founders Say Other Firms Will Soon Follow · Market & press · 2023

qs.q: In our trial, we saw some amazing results.”  ### Fine Tuning by Firm  Pereyra and Weinberg said that they will continue to roll out Harvey on a firm-by-firm basis, as the model requires them to fine tune it for each firm.
qs.a: As Allen & Overy Deploys GPT-based Legal App Harvey Firmwide, Founders Say Other Firms Will Soon Follow · Market & press · 2023

elens.an:
The curated 2025 sources collectively accept the principal proposition and materially develop it with an operational account of adoption at scale. Across vendor, firm, interview and customer-research materials, organisational value is associated with embedding AI in defined legal workflows, organisation-specific knowledge, existing work tools and matter contexts; providing onboarding, customer-success support and guided starting points; establishing human verification, permissions and governance; and translating individual experimentation into repeatable team practices. Several sources further propose concrete routes from engagement to value, including specialised firm-client workflows, analysis of written-off work, revenue-aligned use cases and implementation services for in-house teams.

Material variation concerns both implementation strategy and what counts as evidence. LaBarre advocates identifying use cases and mandating coordinated use, whereas other accounts emphasise guided experimentation, responsive support and product design that reduces behavioural barriers. Some sources treat sustained or broader product use as a useful early signal, and the Harvey-commissioned RSGI study reports higher estimated time savings for self-defined power users. Yet that research also states that usage does not invariably produce savings and that most savings figures are estimates. Pereyra similarly separates high daily activity from financial ROI, arguing that horizontal-assistant use is difficult to map to returns and that practice-specific workflows offer a clearer measurement route.

The evidence base is uneven. Internal examples and customer reports describe time savings, reusable work product and reduced external spending, but these are largely vendor-relayed, estimated or drawn from experienced and technologically advanced customers. Product releases and enterprise announcements demonstrate licences, workflow creation, training targets and deployment commitments, not necessarily quality, productivity or realised financial returns. A&O Shearman’s claimed gains are participant endorsements without independent testing, while Latham’s rollout describes intended rather than completed adoption. Law & Order: GPU adds a caution that prestigious-firm purchasing can be driven by brand and top-down sales even where daily use remains limited. Tara Waters’s excerpt is the exception: it previews adoption-at-scale issues but supplies too little substantive evidence to determine a position. Thus, the period strengthens the proposition mainly by specifying implementation mechanisms and measurement distinctions, while leaving causal, independently validated evidence of organisational value limited.

qs.q: The most common advice I give customers when they ask about how to roll out AI tools is that **organizations need to do more than just provide the tools**.
qs.a: How our In-House Legal Team Uses Harvey to Work Smarter · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: But…  I think a lot of it is localizing it to practice areas because I think the big challenge is when you use Harvey as a horizontal assistant, it’s hard to map this to ROI.
qs.a: The Models Are the Product: Gabe Pereyra on Building an AI Associate and Matter-Centric Workflows · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

elens.an:
The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the principal proposition that organisational value comes from sustained, effective use, workflow redesign and implementation support rather than software purchasing or activity alone. They materially develop it into an operational model: protected experimentation and verification; peer coaching and practice-group champions; legal engineers and specialist support; reusable workflows and agents; integration into existing work environments; and governance for firmwide or cross-organisational deployment. Practitioner accounts report faster review, greater analytical depth and capacity, while customer research associates stronger impact with integration and capability-building. However, much of this evidence consists of vendor material, practitioner self-reports, customer-only commissioned research, product announcements and exploratory testimonials rather than independent causal evaluation.

Material variation concerns what usage data means and how adoption should be driven. Tom Whittaker and Javier Díez Tomillo distinguish frequency from quality, workflow fit and discovery of valuable applications; Andrei Salajan treats sustained voluntary engagement as an initial signal of value, though not sufficient by itself. Some accounts favour mandates, targets or directional usage tracking, whereas others emphasise non-prescriptive experimentation, peer influence and personally experienced benefits. Sources also differ on learning time and user characteristics: Dressler describes a verification-heavy J-curve, while later customer research reports relatively rapid fluency; Díez Tomillo tentatively associates youth and technical fluency with power use, while Bazin reports no generational divide. The period further extends the proposition from individual proficiency to agentic and collaborative infrastructure, but activity counts, launches and deployment commitments do not establish reliable end-to-end performance, realised ROI or client savings. Human verification and institutional governance therefore remain necessary, and billable-hour incentives may prevent time savings from becoming financial value.

qs.q: But measuring [adoption](/blog/turn-ai-adoption-into-firm-wide-change) purely by prompt volume doesn’t reflect quality or outcomes.
qs.a: Harvey Power Users: The Purposeful User — Tom Whittaker at Burges Salmon · Legal-tech vendor · 2026
